item.title: China's satellite internet links Arctic, Antarctica, Qinghai-Tibet Plateau for first time
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 13:30:00
CHINA / SOCIETY China's satellite internet links Arctic, Antarctica, Qinghai-Tibet Plateau for first time By Xinhua Published: Oct 19, 2026 01:30 PM
China's 16th Arctic Ocean expedition team said Monday that its polar icebreaker Jidi had completed a pre-operational application test of domestically developed satellite internet along Arctic shipping routes. During the voyage, networked communications were successfully verified for the first time across the Arctic, Antarctica, and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, also known as the "Third Pole" of Earth, closing the last communications coverage gap in the world, according to the expedition team. The expedition was organized by China's Ministry of Natural Resources.

item.title: China rolls out tech-driven commerce plan to push AI-powered manufacturing, BCI, embodied intelligence commercialization
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 13:18:00
AI face Photo: VCG China’s nine government departments have recently issued a guideline to accelerate technology-driven commerce, rolling out a package of measures to integrate cutting-edge digital tech innovations with commercial services to expand high‑quality supply and foster new consumption driving forces. The overall goal is to upgrade goods consumption, expand service consumption, improve circulation efficiency and foster innovation in integrated consumption scenarios in a coordinated manner. It seeks to scale up the adoption of emerging technologies as it advances intelligent, green and integrated development across the entire commercial chain. The guideline calls for in-depth implementation of the “AI+Manufacturing” special initiative, to deeply embed artificial intelligence into product R&D, design, production and marketing links. Authorities aim to enrich supplies of intelligent consumer goods including smartphones, personal computers, smart home appliances, wearable devices and robots. It prioritizes faster market translation of frontier technologies such as brain-computer interfaces (BCI) and embodied intelligence. China will ramp up R&D of key technologies in new displays and smart terminals, expand real-world application scenarios and viable business models, and scale up demonstration projects. The plan supports building commercial technology innovation hubs and cultivating technology transfer institutions focused on consumer goods. The country will also nurture well-regulated new intelligent service forms including robotic services and virtual human companionship. It backs R&D and industrialization of ultra-high-definition audiovisual technologies, promoting immersive audio-visual experiences in shopping districts, cultural entertainment, tourism and education. AI and digital twin technologies will be deployed to upgrade IP development and design for culture, tourism, sports, national-trend and time-honored industries, enabling cross-sector integration. The document is the first comprehensive and systematic one themed on “technology‑driven commercial development” for the new development stage, aiming to integrate technological innovation throughout the full commercial‑trade chain, officials said. Technological innovation has increasingly become an important driver for expanding and upgrading consumption. Responding to the current new wave of technological and industrial revolution, the document addresses the immediate need to expand consumption and invigorate the consumer market. Meanwhile, it takes a long‑term perspective, leveraging scientific‑technological innovation to upgrade traditional commerce and foster new business forms, so as to deliver sustained impetus for the high‑quality development of commerce and trade, Yuan Xiaoming, an official from MOFCOM said. The policy marks another push to leverage technology to upgrade commerce and consumption, bridging lab breakthroughs with mass-market products and services, while nurturing new growth points for domestic demand, experts said. The tech-driven commerce strategy aims to empower the entire chain spanning production, circulation and consumption. It targets consumer-facing scenarios for both goods and services, with the major goal of creating new supply, fostering fresh consumption drivers and lifting consumer experience, Hu Qimu, a professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, told the Global Times on Monday. Technology and market demand often reinforce each other. Larger market demand spreads upfront R&D costs, helping frontier technologies cross the break-even point and form viable commercial cycles, he said. The policy will help turn technological innovations into new‑form supply, which generates and accommodates market demand. It closes the loop spanning scientific and technological achievements, deliverable products, commercially traded goods and consumption scenarios, Chen Jing, a vice president of the Technology and Strategy Research Institute, told the Global Times on Monday. Rising living standards fuel consumer demand for better quality and experience. MOFCOM data shows smart glasses sales on major e-commerce platforms jumped 110 percent from January to September.

item.title: China's Central Archives opens over 5,000 Long March items to mark 90th anniversary
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 10:10:00
China's Central Archives opens more than 5,000 Long March-related archival items to the public on October 19, 2026 to mark the 90th anniversary of the Red Army's Long March victory. Photo: CCTV News China's Central Archives opened more than 5,000 Long March-related archival items to the public on Monday to mark the 90th anniversary of the Red Army's Long March victory, offering firsthand accounts of key battles, strategic decisions and solidarity between soldiers and civilians, according to China Central Television (CCTV) News. The newly accessible materials mainly date from October 1934 to October 1936, including include programs and declarations issued by the Communist Party of China, Red Army telegrams and reports on operational deployments, and revolutionary newspapers and periodicals founded and published by the Party. Together, they showcase the revolutionary spirit of the CPC and the people's armed forces, vividly depicting how the Red Army and ordinary people stood united, braved sacrifice and pressed ahead during the Long March, according to CCTV News. Among the materials opened to the public for the first time is Jiebao (victory bulletin), a newspaper founded by the CPC's Shanghai central bureau. A total of 40 issues were published between October 1933 and June 1935, exposing the reactionary rule of the Kuomintang, publicizing the Red Army's military achievements and development in the revolutionary base areas. Liu Kun, a staff member of the Central Archives' archival access department, was cited as saying that "the December 17, 1934, issue of Jiebao carried a report stating, 'The westward-bound Red Army has victoriously captured Liping in Guizhou' … Liping was the site of the first Political Bureau meeting held by the CPC Central Committee after the Long March began. The Liping Meeting affirmed the decision to change course at Tongdao and established the Red Army's strategy of advancing westward, thereby averting the risk of being encircled and annihilated by Kuomintang forces had it continued north." The words "utmost urgency" on the telegram testify to the critical military situation at the time. Another document, titled "Report on the first division's covering of the entire army's bridge crossing tomorrow," provides a detailed account of the Red Army's exploits in capturing Luding Bridge, said Liu. "The capture of Luding Bridge was one of the major victories of strategic significance during the Red Army's Long March," Liu said. "As a firsthand battlefield record, this document details when units of the first red army corps arrived at Luding Bridge and launched their attacks. It also records the situation on the ground as they captured the bridge, defeated a regiment of Sichuan troops and seized military supplies. The document states, 'Today, we captured more than 100 prisoners and over 100 firearms, along with enough ammunition and hand grenades to substantially replenish our supplies.'" The 25th Red Army set out from Hejiachong in Luoshan county, Henan Province, on November 16, 1934, and arrived in Yongping, Shaanxi Province, on September 15, 1935, to become the first Red Army force to reach northern Shaanxi during the Long March. A special report submitted to the CPC Central Committee on July 17, 1935, by Wu Huanxian, the political commissar of the 25th Red Army, is an important historical source for research into the force's Long March. "In this report, Wu perceptively raised the question of whether they could join forces with the 26th and 28th armies, concentrate their strength to destroy enemy forces, support the main Red Army's operations in the northwest, and swiftly establish a new, strong and consolidated revolutionary base there," Liu said. "Operating in isolation, without instructions from the CPC Central Committee or deployments ordered by higher authorities, the CPC Hubei-Henan-Shaanxi Provincial Committee resolutely decided that the main force of the 25th Red Army should advance westward and northward to support the main Red Army. Wu's report also explains the thinking behind that decision," Liu said. Starting Monday, audiences can consult these materials at the Central Archives' public reading hall by presenting valid identification, such as a national ID card or work ID, per CCTV News. Global Times

item.title: China's GDP expands 4.6% year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026, on track to meet pre-set annual growth target
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 10:03:00
Photo: Li Xuanmin/Global Times China’s GDP expanded 4.6 percent year-on-year to reach 107.11 trillion yuan ($16 trillion) in the first nine months, data from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed on Monday. The freshly-released figure landed well within the annual GDP growth target of around 4.5 percent to 5 percent for this year, showing that the world’s second largest economy continues to operate on the sound trajectory, setting a solid foundation for achieving the full-year growth target, analysts said. In the third quarter, China’s GDP grew 4.5 percent year-on-year , accelerating from the 4.3-percent growth recorded in the second quarter. In the first quarter, China’s GDP jumped 5 percent, NBS data showed. Observers said the third-quarter reading reflects multiple factors, including the manufacturing strength of China’s high-tech and equipment sectors, which continued to underpin robust external demand, the strong drive from new and emerging industries, as well as the steady progress in the course of high-quality development. Despite mounting uncertainties, Chinese analysts anticipated that the fourth-quarter reading would further pick up as more policy measures take effect and strong manufacturing momentum persists. According to the NBS data, China's value-added industrial output of above-scale enterprises in the first nine months rose 5.3 percent compared to the same period in 2025, while fixed-asset investment dropped by 7.2 percent year-on-year. China's total retail sales of consumer goods expanded by 2.6 percent year-on-year in the January-September period, according to the NBS data. “Despite facing downward pressures from both domestic and external factors, the Chinese economy demonstrated a clear trend of high-quality development in the first three quarters, with growth momentum shifting toward new drivers and the economic structure continuing to improve,” Hu Qimu, a professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, told the Global Times. Tian Yun, a Beijing-based veteran economist, told the Global Times that China’s resilient production and relatively rapid export growth have played an important role in boosting the economy in the third quarter, especially in the manufacturing of high-tech products related to artificial intelligence (AI). “The figure has highlighted China’s role as a stabilizer and locomotive of the global supply chain, and such position could be further strengthened in the fourth quarter, taking account of rising geopolitical tensions and external uncertainties,” Tian said. He stressed that the country’s resilient, stable and complete industrial chain has also helped cushion the global economy against some short-term disruptions, including those linked to the Strait of Hormuz. In the third quarter, while internal demand continued to recover, economists pointed to more signs of improvement in September, suggesting that policy support and seasonal factors were beginning to take effect and reinforcing the economy’s underlying resilience. Analysts attributed the improvement partly to the earlier timing of the Mid-Autumn Festival, which lifted spending on essential goods, alongside support from “more proactive and effective” macro policies, which effectively address multiple challenges and a low base effect from last year. They expected the accelerated implementation of existing policies to further stabilize domestic demand and market expectations in the fourth quarter. “In fact, China’s contribution to the global market today is not simply a matter of how large a share of global GDP it accounts for. It is now the world’s second-largest consumer market, indicating its important role as a major source of demand and the enormous development opportunities it offers to the world,” Tiansaid. In first three quarters of the year, China's foreign trade growth hit five-year high , with exports jumping 16.4 percent while imports expanded 22.3 percent, customs data showed. Observers believed that the economic operation in the first nine months has set the tone for the country to achieve the full-year GDP growth target of 4.5 to 5 percent, with growth momentum – in particular new drivers from AI and high-tech manufacturing – expected to further consolidate in the fourth quarter. “As the government’s countercyclical adjustments ramp up, incremental policies are rolled out in succession, and industrial transformation and upgrading further gain steam, the economy is expected to maintain a steady and resilient trajectory throughout the year,” Hu said. item.title: Liangzhu forum opens, highlights heritage conservation, int'l cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 08:20:00
Lina Mendoni, Minister of Culture of Greece, addresses the opening ceremony of the fourth Liangzhu Forum in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, Oct. 18, 2026. The fourth Liangzhu Forum opened Sunday in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, to discuss challenges in cultural heritage conservation and paths to deepen international cooperation. The year 2026 marks the 90th anniversary of the discovery of the Liangzhu ruins. Themed "Bridging the Past and the Future: Safeguarding Cultural Heritage for Our Times," the forum brings together officials, archaeologists and scholars from around the world. (Xinhua/Xu Yu) The fourth Liangzhu Forum opened Sunday in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, to discuss challenges in cultural heritage conservation and paths to deepen international cooperation. The year 2026 marks the 90th anniversary of the discovery of the Liangzhu ruins. Themed "Bridging the Past and the Future: Safeguarding Cultural Heritage for Our Times," the forum brings together officials, archaeologists and scholars from around the world. Experts and scholars will discuss topics ranging from early civilizations to archaeological research on ancient cities, with new research findings and advances also set to be unveiled, Zhang Ling, an official with China's National Cultural Heritage Administration, said at an earlier briefing. Participants will address challenges including the loss of cultural heritage, advances in technologies for protecting and utilizing cultural relics, and sustainable tourism, Zhang added. Lina Mendoni, Minister of Culture of Greece, said in a speech at the opening ceremony that people must move beyond traditional approaches and adopt adaptive, preventive and holistic management to safeguard cultural heritage. "UNESCO believes that sustainable tourism can help safeguard cultural heritage by raising awareness of the importance of heritage for future generations, improving cultural understanding and strengthening local livelihoods," said Nayef Al-Fayez, UNESCO Assistant Director-General for Culture, in his video speech. The forum brings together four international organizations: UNESCO, based in Paris; the International Centre for the Study of the Preservation and Restoration of Cultural Property, headquartered in Rome; the Alliance for Cultural Heritage in Asia, based in Beijing; and the International Alliance for the Protection of Heritage, headquartered in Geneva. The gathering marks a step for the forum to turn into a broader venue for multilateral dialogue on cultural heritage, said Wen Dayan, another official with the National Cultural Heritage Administration. This year's event includes an opening ceremony and main forum, five sub-forums and five companion events, including an international artists' creative tour exhibition, a Liangzhu cultural and creative market, a design exhibition and international dialogues. Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2019, the Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City offer important evidence of an early regional state that flourished more than 5,000 years ago. The inaugural forum was held in Hangzhou in 2023. The fourth edition runs through Tuesday and is co-hosted by China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism, the National Cultural Heritage Administration and the Zhejiang provincial government. item.title: The Takaichi government is increasingly resembling an extremist cult: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 23:53:00
Militaristic emblem Illustration: Liu Rui/GT It is precisely because the Takaichi government has tolerated and encouraged these forces that right-wing elements in Japanese politics are becoming more brazen than ever. They have even constructed a narrative of a "holy war for history," attempting to repackage the specter of militarism as a "spiritual legacy" of which the Japanese people should be proud. An increasingly dangerous Japan has long been on the radar of its neighbors, who remain wary of its actions. On Saturday, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made an offering to the Yasukuni Shrine as prime minister. This marked the fourth time this year that Takaichi had made an offering or donated ritual funds to the war criminals' shrine, a frequency rarely seen among Japan's former prime ministers. On the same day, several cabinet ministers and lawmakers also visited the shrine to pay their respects. The pattern of "the prime minister sending offerings while her subordinates make the pilgrimage" is becoming a familiar ritual in Takaichi's cabinet. Some Japanese right-wing figures argue that Takaichi has not visited the shrine in her capacity as prime minister since taking office, as if this were sufficient to address concerns over Japan's historical record. Yet Takaichi refrains from visiting in person while making offerings in the name of the prime minister; cabinet ministers and senior Liberal Democratic Party officials make the pilgrimage on her behalf, while she pays her respects from afar. Tokyo is pursuing an opportunistic strategy: Preserving its right-wing support base, avoiding the political fallout of a direct visit, and exploiting historical revisionism to justify military expansion and preparations for war. In fact, during nearly a year in office, Takaichi has consistently sent signals to Japan's domestic right-wing forces, seeking to systematically erode the postwar consensus against war, undermine the legitimacy of Japan's pacifist constitution, and lay the psychological groundwork for constitutional revision, military buildup, and arms expansion. The Takaichi government seems particularly fond of such deceptive tactics. Japan has repeatedly sent the wrong signals on the Taiwan question, effectively closing the door to dialogue while proclaiming internationally that it is "willing to communicate with China." More recently, Takaichi has described China as an "important neighbor" while refusing to retract her erroneous remarks on the Taiwan question. On the one hand, she is publicly putting on a show of eagerness to travel to Shenzhen to attend the APEC meeting. On the other, she is staging a political charade of her own, hinting that the Diet might not approve her attendance. These deceptive maneuvers are, in essence, attempts to exploit ambiguities and find room to maneuver for Tokyo's risky drive toward remilitarization. It is precisely because the Takaichi government has tolerated and encouraged these forces that right-wing elements in Japanese politics are becoming more brazen than ever. They have even constructed a narrative of a "holy war for history," attempting to recast Japan's war of aggression during World War II as a supposedly righteous campaign to "liberate Asia" and portray Class-A war criminals, whose hands were stained with the blood of people across Asia, as "spirits of the war dead who sacrificed themselves for their country." Cabinet members and lawmakers under Takaichi's government frequently visit sites associated with war criminals, using their political power to lend legitimacy to this "holy war" narrative and whip up public support for military expansion and preparations for war. Through repeated offerings, shrine visits, and a sustained propaganda campaign, they seek to gradually erase the just verdicts of the Tokyo Trial and repackage the specter of militarism as a "spiritual legacy" of which the Japanese people should be proud. More alarming still, this "holy war for history" narrative is closely intertwined with the Takaichi government's efforts to revise Japan's pacifist constitution and dramatically expand its military capabilities and preparations for war. This exposes the Takaichi government's deeply extremist, cult-like nature. Once historical responsibility for wartime atrocities is recast as "national sacrifice," the pacifist constitution can be portrayed as "a shackle holding back the nation's development," and military expansion and preparations for war can be given a supposedly "legitimate" justification. The erosion of historical understanding ultimately leads to a shift in national security strategy. This is precisely the most insidious and dangerous path toward Japan's remilitarization. Japanese politicians have openly discussed introducing nuclear-powered submarines and allowing US forces to bring nuclear weapons into Japan, while the "Three Non-Nuclear Principles" - a cornerstone of Japan's postwar nuclear policy commitments to the international community - have come under increasing pressure. Some Japanese right-wing figures believe they can blur the line between history and present-day realities, invoke "threats from neighboring countries" as a pretext for military expansion, and dress up that expansion as a reasonable national security measure. They seem to think this will allow them to pull the wool over the world's eyes and dismantle the postwar order in its entirety under the international community's very nose. But since Takaichi took office, Japan's relations with neighboring countries have deteriorated sharply. China, South Korea, and other countries that suffered under Japanese aggression have repeatedly lodged strong protests over her shrine-related actions and historically revisionist remarks, while expressing clear concerns about her moves to push beyond Japan's established exclusively defense-oriented policy. Russia and North Korea, too, remain highly vigilant about Japan's military buildup, preparations for war, and efforts to repudiate the postwar order, having issued explicit warnings through diplomatic channels on multiple occasions. An increasingly dangerous Japan has long been on the radar of its neighbors, who remain wary of its actions. Tokyo will find it far from easy to get away with its "deception tactics." Masahiko Shimizu, a professor of constitutional law at Nippon Sport Science University, has bluntly stated that Japanese politicians visiting Yasukuni Shrine is akin to German leaders tending Adolf Hitler's grave - a blatant desecration of historical justice. The analogy may not be entirely precise, but it is one that the US and Western public opinion, which have long tolerated the rhetoric and actions of Japan's right wing and even lent credibility to Japan's "peaceful" facade, would do well to heed. The 14 Class-A war criminals from WWII were convicted of war crimes by an international tribunal in accordance with the law. The wars of aggression they planned, launched, and carried out inflicted immense suffering on countries across Asia. As long as Japanese politicians continue to pay homage to these war criminals, this chapter of history can absolutely not truly be closed. No matter how the Takaichi government tries to repackage its actions or twist the facts, any attempt to whitewash militarism or resume military expansion will ultimately expose its dangerous nature before the entire world, provoking resolute opposition and ending in complete failure.

item.title: When 'strategic partner' means different things in Washington and New Delhi
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 22:19:00
US, India Illustration:Chen Xia/GT The US-India relationship has once again laid bare the exercise of great power leverage - Washington is playing an ancient game: first using strategic commitments to take you hostage, then using economic coercion to suppress you. Indian media reports say US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is about to visit India, marking his second visit this year. Washington wants to talk about a "strategic partnership," while New Delhi wants to talk about tariffs. The two sides are working from completely different menus. Nine months have passed, and the US-India trade framework agreement reached in February remains unsigned. India's finance minister says negotiations have hit a "plateau." The US Trade Representative says an announcement is "not imminent." Translation: they're stuck, and neither side is willing to budge further. Washington's rhetoric has always been polished. Through references to the "Indo-Pacific Strategy", shared values and the Quad - Washington portrays India as its most trusted partner in the Asia-Pacific. But when it comes to trade realities, the tone shifts: high tariffs on Indian steel, sustained pressure on Indian pharmaceuticals, barriers against Indian IT services. Meanwhile, Japan, South Korea, and Australia are receiving far more favorable treatment during the same period. This tells us a lot about the problem. Washington ranks its "strategic partners" by usefulness. When it needs India to take sides in the Indo-Pacific, it calls you a partner; when it needs to protect its own industries, the tariff club swings freely. Japan and South Korea are military allies; Australia is part of the "Five Eyes"; India, in Washington's ledger, is simply a card whose value can be adjusted at any time. What particularly alarms New Delhi is that the current US administration is demanding that India take three major steps: reduce Russian oil purchases, open agricultural markets, and increase American energy imports. And reportedly, this time they want India to buy more Venezuelan oil - oil over which the US has already established monopoly control. Each demand is no minor matter. Energy security affects the nation's lifeline; agriculture involves the livelihoods of hundreds of millions of small farmers; Russian oil helps keep costs down for Indian industry. US' subtext is clear: You must play by my rules. It's hard to believe such demands come from a "partner." Of course, the US has long used geopolitical leverage to "manipulate" its relationship with India, using the Quad and the "Indo-Pacific Strategy" to reinforce India's position while trying to restrict India's room for maneuver. But India has not fully accepted the hand dealt. For India, the value of being designated an American "strategic partner" is diminishing. Meanwhile, with tariff policies mired in legal challenges, India is even more hesitant to make commitments - will policy change again next year? India's exports have grown strongly in 2026. If American tariffs rise back to 25 percent, that growth trajectory will be destroyed. India would rather not sign an agreement than accept terms that damage its long-term prospects. So the situation has become this: the US applies pressure; India drags its feet. The delay is not passive submission - it is a form of resistance with boundaries. India cannot easily abandon US' security card, but it refuses to put all its chips on the table. The trade agreement remains unsigned for this reason. Whether this agreement gets signed or not, India has already seen through America's real agenda. Behind this lies a larger question: What does Washington's "strategic partnership" actually offer India? India's example makes the answer clear. The US doesn't want an equal partner - it wants a partner willing to follow its strategic lead and sacrifice economic interests on American terms. The moment the other side's interests conflict with American domestic politics, "partnership" gives way to tariffs. Such a relationship is difficult for any nation conscious of its own interests to accept long-term. For India, the American "strategic partner" label is losing value. This doesn't mean India will turn toward some other great power. Still, it means New Delhi will more firmly chart its own course, strengthen ties with Russia, Iran, and others, and place "strategic autonomy" more prominently in its dealings with major powers. The deadlock in US-India trade negotiations is more than a commercial dispute. It exposes the limits of a model of relations between major powers: prioritizing exploitation over equality; demanding cooperation while denying respect. How far such a relationship can go - India is answering that question in its own way.

item.title: GT Voice: India should move beyond deficit anxiety as trade with China rises
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 21:03:00
China, India Illustration: Xia Qing/GT The latest China-India trade figures again thrusts the economic relationship into the media spotlight. India's bilateral trade with China rose nearly 29 percent year-on-year to reach $91.76 billion in the April-September period, making China the largest trading partner of India in the first half of the 2026-27 financial year, according to India's Commerce Ministry. The rising momentum of China-India trade is a positive development both sides should treasure. Yet behind the impressive numbers, India's anxiety about its trade deficit with China remains clearly visible. Frankly speaking, India's long-running trade deficit with China is a structural phenomenon shaped over the years by the two countries' industrial structures and comparative advantages. India is by no means short of competitive industries. From its fast-rising electronics assembly capacity to globally recognized pharmaceutical intermediate products, specialty agricultural products and textile goods, India holds a lot of cards that it can use to compete internationally. But having competitive industries is not the same as delivering a surge in exports to China. For a very long time, the basic pattern of China-India trade saw China ship large volumes of electromechanical equipment, electronic components and industrial intermediates to India, while India exported iron ore, seafood and other resource-based and primary goods to China. This division of labor was the natural outcome of the two countries' different stages of industrialization. If India wants to gradually ease its trade deficit, the key lies in tapping its own potential and turning its competitive industries into products that the Chinese market demands. What makes this moment different is that China's ongoing push for high-end, intelligent manufacturing upgrading and continued opening-up of its services sectors have opened unprecedented new window of opportunities for India. The massive new demand generated across these fields can easily become the core direction for India to cultivate new export growth points to China. Rather than competing for shares in traditional primary product categories, aligning export portfolios with the trajectory of China's industrial upgrade represents a more pragmatic and sustainable path forward. Signs of progress in this direction are emerging. According to Chinese customs data, China's imports from India surged 40.7 percent year-on-year in the January-September period, far outpacing average trade growth. This clearly shows that India's exports to China are gradually finding a direction suited to the Chinese market. The real question before India is whether it can sustain this round of growth, extend breakthroughs in a few sectors to more industrial tracks, and turn short-term export gains into long-term domestic manufacturing competitiveness. Some in India simply attribute the trade deficit with China to market access issues, and even go so far as to claim that "non-tariff barriers remain the biggest obstacle" to bilateral trade. But if access to the Chinese market was riddled with barriers to the extent that some claim, how could India's exports to China have grown by more than 40 percent? Viewed from another perspective, such voices actually reflect a growing awareness across Indian circles of how important the Chinese market is to the future of Indian manufacturing, along with a strong eagerness among Indian exporters to expand their footprint in China. China's overall level of opening-up has been substantial, and India's high export growth was delivered under the current open trade framework ̵ a fact that speaks far louder than any debate. Blaming trade deficit entirely on alleged external barriers risks covering up real shortcomings in product competitiveness, channel development, and international standard alignment. This approach does nothing to solve the actual problem, and will only work against the healthy development of bilateral trade relations. In the long run, there remains ample room to deepen China-India economic cooperation, and the two sides can certainly move forward together on the basis of mutual benefit and reciprocity to make the pie bigger. The economic relationship between two countries should not be defined by a single deficit figure. Volumes are rising, exports are growing, and the willingness of both sides to expand cooperation is strengthening, which are all encouraging signs. What needs to be done is to let the potential continue to materialize and make mutual benefit and reciprocity the shared guiding principles.

item.title: 17th Media Forum China-Germany held in Heidelberg, stressing media role in strengthening China-Germany relations
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18 18:15:00
The 17th Media Forum China-Germany hosted by the Global Times is held in Heidelberg, Germany, from October 14 to 16, 2026. The 17th Media Forum China-Germany, hosted by the Global Times, was held in Heidelberg, Germany, from October 14 to 16. The forum serves as an important platform for strengthening media ties, fostering mutual understanding and exploring how the press can contribute to the healthy and stable development of China-Germany relations. Senior journalists, leaders of major media organizations, and experts and scholars from China and Germany, gathered on the banks of the Neckar River for in-depth discussions on 10 topics, including China-Germany relations, global security, artificial intelligence governance, economic and trade cooperation, green development, global governance and media responsibility. They actively explored shared interests between China and Germany in areas such as trade and investment, technological development, green development and media cooperation, seeking new approaches to deepening mutual understanding and cooperation amid a complex international landscape. Changes in the global landscape unseen in a century are accelerating now, while challenges such as geopolitical conflicts and trade protectionism are becoming increasingly intertwined. As two of the world's major economies, China and Germany maintain close ties in trade and investment, science and technology, and the green transition. Their bilateral relationship is important not only to the development of the two countries, but also to China-Europe cooperation and global economic stability. Against the backdrop of a complex and changing international situation and persistent differences in perceptions, strengthening direct dialogue and fostering mutual understanding and trust have become particularly important. In February, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited China with a business delegation. The leaders of the two countries exchanged views on China-Germany relations, international and regional issues, and economic policies. Both sides agreed to promote the continuous new development of the all-round strategic partnership, promote dialogue and cooperation and uphold multilateralism and free trade. The bilateral relationship not only bears on the interests of both countries, but also has significant impact on Europe and the world. Subsequently, several German ministers visited China in succession, sustaining the momentum of high-level exchanges and advancing deeper cooperation. At the second meeting of the China-EU Trade and Investment Consultation Mechanism, held from October 8 to 9 in Beijing, China and the EU reached a 16-point consensus covering trade and investment, export controls, intellectual property rights and World Trade Organization (WTO) reform during high-level talks in Beijing on Thursday and Friday, marking concrete progress in efforts to manage bilateral economic differences. Against this backdrop, the 17th Media Forum China-Germany aims to further strengthen the role of the media in both countries as a bridge for communication. Through face-to-face exchanges, it seeks to enhance mutual understanding and trust, objectively present areas of consensus and differences between the two sides on major international issues, and expand opportunities for cooperation between Chinese and German media through mutual respect and candid dialogue. It also provides a platform for bringing the peoples of the two countries closer together and bridging gaps in mutual perceptions. In his opening remarks, Bai Long, deputy editor-in-chief of the Global Times, said that the Media Forum China-Germany has been held for 17 sessions and that cooperation between China and Germany has long been characterized by deeply interconnected interests, with each side having a stake in the other. In his view, the pens and cameras in the hands of media professionals can create divergent perceptions, but they can also build bridges of understanding. Bai called for diverse perspectives to be tested and refined through debate to produce sound insights, strengthen mutual trust between China and Germany and between China and Europe, and contribute the media community's voice of reason to the world. During the forum, discussions among Chinese and German participants addressed differences in their understanding of the international situation and industrial policies, while also examining their shared practical interests in technological innovation, the green transition and multilateral cooperation. From debates over the broader international order to specific industrial partnerships and journalistic practices, the exchanges helped clarify each side's concerns and gave more concrete meaning to the shared goal of cooperation. Since its launch in 2010, the Media Forum China-Germany has been held for 17 consecutive sessions and has gradually become an important platform for high-level dialogue and mutual understanding among major media organizations in the two countries. In the face of profound changes in the international landscape, the roundtable will continue to serve as a bridge for communication, promote deeper exchanges and cooperation between Chinese and German media, and inject more constructive momentum into the sound and stable development of bilateral relations. Meanwhile, the Global Times "Overseas China Week" photo exhibition also came to Heidelberg. During the media forum, the photo exhibition titled "Green and Innovation: China and Germany Embarking on Vibrant Future" was successfully held. The "Overseas China Week" is an international cultural communication and dialogue initiative launched by the Global Times to promote cross-cultural exchanges, mutual learning among civilizations, and media cooperation with other countries. The initiative has previously held themed exhibitions and promotional activities in Kazakhstan, Argentina, Brazil, South Korea, South Africa and Kyrgyzstan, receiving positive responses.
